texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 1. Proactively take control of your time and efforts
texts.text: 1. Proactively take control of your time and efforts

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Burnout conquerors keep a keen eye on how they spend their time and energy at work to make sure they’re working smarter, not harder. An open block in their calendar to do deep work isn’t just going to drop in from the sky. Their most productive hours aren’t going to magically become available for priority work. Burnout conquerors make their days their own.
texts.text: Burnout conquerors keep a keen eye on how they spend their time and energy at work to make sure they’re working smarter, not harder. An open block in their calendar to do deep work isn’t just going to drop in from the sky. Their most productive hours aren’t going to magically become available for priority work. Burnout conquerors make their days their own.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: “For me, burnout happens when I become ineffective at my job, no matter how many hours I put in. When I start to feel like I’m not making progress, I immediately start examining why. A perfect example is right now—I’ve not moved the needle with my priorities in weeks. There’s been a lot of firefighting, but nothing proactive. I started to examine what I’m spending time on and how I can pivot to spending time on what I should be doing. Calendar audit was step #1, declined meetings I really didn’t need to be in, blocked off heads-down time, and, in a matter of days, I’m back on track.”

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Burnout conquerors don’t accept conventional organizational expectations of employees. They don’t buy into the common corporate narrative that puts the onus on employees to deal with burnout. And they don’t feel guilty if they’re feeling bad or in need of a break. The people who are actively preventing burnout have a strong belief system that insulates them from falling victim to burnout-related organizational mind games. Here’s how:
texts.text: Burnout conquerors don’t accept conventional organizational expectations of employees. They don’t buy into the common corporate narrative that puts the onus on employees to deal with burnout. And they don’t feel guilty if they’re feeling bad or in need of a break. The people who are actively preventing burnout have a strong belief system that insulates them from falling victim to burnout-related organizational mind games. Here’s how:

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 1. Understand that burnout isn’t your fault
texts.text: 1. Understand that burnout isn’t your fault

texts.label: text
texts.orig: While burnout conquerors take actionable steps toward preventing burnout in their own lives, they also know that the kind of deep exhaustion so many in the industry are feeling should not be blamed on the people suffering from it. Burnout is “organizational warfare,” not a personal responsibility.
texts.text: While burnout conquerors take actionable steps toward preventing burnout in their own lives, they also know that the kind of deep exhaustion so many in the industry are feeling should not be blamed on the people suffering from it. Burnout is “organizational warfare,” not a personal responsibility.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: “I’m super-annoyed by the common expectation that you have to deal with your burnout on your own, as if it’s a personal problem and not an organisational problem. Burnout is not a personality problem; it’s a result of broken processes, unclear expectations, bad incentives (e.g. dumb performance review cycles and expectations), and poor work conditions . . . and no, those free-pizza Fridays and free mental health sessions are not company benefits. They are band-aids and signs of serious organisational dysfunction.”

texts.orig: 3. Feel feelings instead of optimizing them away
texts.text: 3. Feel feelings instead of optimizing them away

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Burnout conquerors don’t buy into the optimization culture of tech. When bad feelings arrive—and they always do at some point—they know it’s never more efficient to push them away to try to maximize consistent output. Instead, as one respondent says, “sometimes you need to just be human and feel terrible for a while.”

texts.label: text
texts.orig: “Generally, all advice sounds really good in theory, but it’s really hard to put it into practice, especially if people are already under pressure. Telling someone who needs rest to exercise regularly can just add to their stress . . . I think sometimes we just need to also fully feel what we feel—if we’re stressed, acknowledge that; if you need to cry, cry; if you need to take a couple of days to just lie on the couch and eat bad food, do it. As long as you set a light at the end of the tunnel for yourself.”
